title: Four Lakes of Zendia
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: Lakes are among the most sensitive indicators of change in the natural world. Their level goes up when the rains are heavy and falls in times of drought, and it can also be altered by human actions such as building dams or taking water for farms. In the imaginary island nation of Zendia, scientists have measured the water level in four important lakes every month for twenty years, and their records show four very different patterns. This passage describes each lake in turn and then discusses what the pattern teaches us about managing water, a question of growing importance for many countries.

Lake Aru lies in the north of the island and is fed by melting snow from the mountains. Its level has risen slowly but steadily throughout the twenty years, by roughly a metre in all. Scientists believe that the cause is warmer weather, which has caused the glaciers to melt faster and sent more water into the streams that feed the lake. This may sound like good news, but it is not entirely so: villages on the shore have been flooded several times, and farmers have lost fields that had been used for generations. The glaciers will not last for ever, and the lake is expected to shrink when the ice is gone.

Lake Bellu followed a different course. For the first seven years, its level fell, as a long drought dried up the rivers that feed it and farmers took water from its shores for irrigation. At its lowest point, the lake was less than half its former size, and the fishing boats lay on dry mud. Then the rains returned, the government limited the amount of water that farms could take, and the level rose again, until by the end of the twenty years it was nearly as high as it had been at the start. The recovery surprised the scientists, who had feared that the damage would be permanent.

The level of Lake Cora has gone up and down without any lasting trend. In the wet season it rises by several metres, and in the dry season it falls again, and the pattern has repeated itself year after year. The lake has no dam and no towns on its shore, and people leave it alone, so it behaves as nature intended. Biologists value it for exactly this reason, because the rising water floods the surrounding forest each year and carries nutrients to the fish that breed there. They call it a healthy lake, and they use it as a standard against which to judge the others.

Lake Dalu provides the sharpest contrast. Its level stayed almost constant for twelve years, and then suddenly dropped by more than three metres in a single season, after engineers opened a new canal to carry water from the lake to a city in the south. The level has remained at the lower height ever since. The canal supplies drinking water to nearly a million people, which is a great benefit, but the lower lake has damaged the wetlands at its edge, and several species of bird that nested there have disappeared. The government says that the city's need for water had to come first.

Dr Tomas Lindqvist, a hydrologist who has studied all four lakes, believes that they show how a lake's level can be changed in different ways: slowly, by the climate; temporarily, by drought; regularly, by the seasons; and suddenly, by human decisions. He argues that the last kind is the most dangerous, because it gives nature no time to adjust. A slow change can be followed and prepared for, but a sudden one may destroy habitats before anyone has noticed what is happening. He therefore urges the government to study the effects of every large project before it is approved.

The government has responded by promising a new law, under which any scheme to take large amounts of water from a lake must be studied for two years before work may begin. Environmental groups welcome the plan but say that it should have been introduced earlier. The government also intends to continue the monthly measurements, which have already proved their value. A new instrument, placed in each lake next year, will send readings directly to a central computer, so that scientists can see the level at any moment without travelling to the shore.
